The 21 home runs at A give him real leverage, but the translation knocks the ISO to .133, and the K% inflates to 29.7% against an MLB baseline of 22.0%. If the walk rate holds when pitchers stop giving him anything to pull and the strikeouts don't compound further, he's a low-end regular with a useful OBP; if the contact doesn't develop, the walks become the one thing keeping him on a roster.

828672_pitcher.text: Jagger Beck is a 19-year-old right-hander generating swing-and-miss at a strong rate—11.7 K/9 ranks 80th percentile in the ValuCast pitcher pool—while maintaining excellent K-BB% (21.6%, 90th percentile) through tight walk control at 3.6 BB/9. The chief risk is that MLB translation downgrades his strikeout rate meaningfully to 8.2 K/9, closing the skill gap between him and average, while his walk rate ticks up to 3.9 BB/9 in the majors. This is a 40-inning sample in active play, so the read reflects early-season feel without the depth of conviction that comes with volume.

828685_hitter.text: The .389 OBP at A-ball is loud for a 19-year-old, and 40 walks in 312 plate appearances tells you the approach is genuine. The problem is the translation: that contact rate and the modest raw power leave his MLB-equivalent ISO at .119, and the MLB average sits at .150, which is a first baseman who can't carry the position. Gray's ceiling lives entirely in whether the power develops enough to close that gap, because the profile as constructed, good eye, fringe thump, first base only, runs out of floor well short of an everyday job.

828824_hitter.text: The surface numbers are loud: .432 OBP, 36 stolen bases, 24 home runs across AA & A+, all in 497 plate appearances at 22. His walk rate translates more cleanly, to 12.7% against an MLB average of 8.5%, so the plate discipline isn't a mirage, but the hit tool is the hinge: if the BABIP regresses hard and the strikeouts don't come down, the average evaporates and you're left with a high-walk, high-strikeout center fielder whose ISO translates to .176. The whole profile points to a bench outfielder or depth piece rather than an everyday player, and at prospect rank 498 he's being valued accordingly.

829033_hitter.text: The .388 OBP at A-ball is the loud number here, and at 18 it earns a second look. Sixty-one walks against 94 strikeouts across 439 plate appearances is a discipline profile most teenagers don't carry, and the translated walk rate of 10.1% compares favorably to an MLB average of 8.5% — suggesting at least some of it survives the jump. The problem is the ISO: .126 at A, translating to .099 at the MLB level against a landscape where .150 is ordinary, which means the on-base skill has to do most of the carrying if he's ever to be more than an organizational piece. If the gap power never fills in as he physically matures, you're looking at a bench bat with a good eye and 28 stolen bases, nothing worse but nothing more.

829034_hitter.text: The .444 OBP at A-ball is loud, but a .439 BABIP is doing most of the carrying. Gonzalez is 19, posting a 1.01 OPS across 153 plate appearances, with 21 walks against 30 strikeouts and 13 stolen bases, so the athletic and zone-feel indicators are both pointing the right direction for his age. The MLB-equivalent translation softens the bat considerably, the ISO dropping from .209 at A to .139, while the MLB average sits at .150, suggesting the in-game power hasn't shown up yet in translation. If the contact rates hold as the BABIP normalizes, he's either a low-end regular or a good bench bat; if they don't, organizational depth is the ceiling, and prospect rank 240 tells you the industry isn't pricing in a different outcome.

829037_hitter.text: The contact and the legs are already there at 18. Across 443 plate appearances at A ball, Alvarez is hitting .261/.343/.429 with 17 stolen bases, and his 18% strikeout rate ranks in the 82nd percentile among the hitter pool, a genuine skill at his age on a real sample. The translation is the problem: that .168 ISO at A ball shrinks to .116 in MLB-equivalent context, a number that sits noticeably short of where average power lands, and an 8% walk rate doesn't add enough margin to paper over thin game power. If the power develops, and at 18 in full-season ball there's room to dream, he's a second-division regular with speed and a real hit tool; if it doesn't, he's a bench piece who runs well and makes contact, which isn't nothing, but it's the ceiling not the floor.

829052_hitter.text: Breyson Guedez is a young left-handed hitter working through strikeout noise at the A level, flashing contact ability (.282 avg, 83rd percentile) but generating minimal power (.119 ISO, 31st percentile) and very little leverage on base (6.6% BB rate, 8th percentile). At 18 with only 272 plate appearances, the strikeout rate (29%) sits just above major-league average in the translation, a concerning baseline for someone still learning pitch recognition. The hit tool is real, but without secondary skills or early power development, the path to impact is narrow.

829058_hitter.text: Gabriel Davalillo is an 18-year-old third baseman showing mixed bat discipline and pop: he's posting .267/.348/.410 with an 11% walk rate and .143 ISO over 227 A-ball plate appearances, though both his strikeout rate (25.6%) and isolated power rank near the middle of the minor-league field. The real concern is that his average and slugging power lag below the tools expected at the position—his .267 AVG is strong for his age, but ISO in the 47th percentile signals he hasn't yet connected the bat to game power. The sample is current and meaningful, but at 18 with moderate command and modest thump so far, this looks like a years-away organizational depth profile rather than a near-term contributor.

829210_hitter.text: Ty Harvey is a 19-year-old catcher showing early discipline at the plate—19% BB% on a 58 PA sample—but swinging and missing at a concerning clip (24.1% K%). His .107 ISO translates to below-average raw power for a catcher, and the strikeout rate (24.1%), even accounting for youth, sits above league average in the MLB equivalent read. The sample is small and fresh, so expect volatility as he faces stiffer velocity and sequencing.

829398_hitter.text: The contact and plate discipline are genuinely loud for a 19-year-old catcher: .329/.466/.494 at A with a 11% strikeout rate that translates to 18.5% at the MLB level, and 26 walks against only 23 strikeouts in 206 plate appearances. The power is the honest gap, with an ISO of .165 at A that softens to a .124 MLB-equivalent, well short of where you'd want it. If the hit tool and walk rate carry through the levels but the power stays modest, you're looking at a bench piece with real on-base value; if he adds even average pull-side pop as he fills out physically, the profile gets more interesting, and catchers who control the zone this well at 19 earn that conversation.

829741_hitter.text: The walk rate is the lead. 829854_hitter.text: Luis Arana is an 18-year-old A-level shortstop who commands the strike zone exceptionally—posting 19.2% BB% over 78 PA—but whose overall bat lacks impact, evidenced by a modest .127 ISO and a .460 SLG despite the strong .462 OBP. The approach grade is elite relative to his peer group; the hit tool is solid; but power and overall impact are well below average, and that power ceiling is the central constraint. At 78 plate appearances in a current season sample, confidence in the profile is limited, though the plate discipline suggests a repeatable skill.

830239_hitter.text: The ISO is the argument: .243 at A+ over 331 plate appearances, which translates to .159 at the MLB level, right at league average for raw power despite coming from a 22-year-old center fielder. What complicates it is the 27% strikeout rate, because that translates to 29.5% against big-league pitching, and a hit tool that grades 55 can carry a 27% K-rate in the minors long before it can carry one against advanced arms. If the contact holds, Walton profiles as a low-end everyday regular with speed-and-power upside; if pitchers find the hole, what's left is a bench bat with real pop.

830336_pitcher.text: The 2.1 ERA across A+ & A is the loud number, but what makes it worth taking seriously is the shape behind it: 87 strikeouts in 64.3 innings with only 19 walks, a 0.9 WHIP, a K-BB% of 27 that ranks at the 98th percentile in his pool. Strip that down to what it translates to at the MLB level and it deflates quickly — the strikeout rate comes out to 8.4 per nine, essentially matching what an average major-league arm produces, and the walk rate lands in the same neighborhood, so the margins that look dominant in A-ball basically become a league-average pitcher. That's the whole profile: the stuff plays up in the lower minors, and if it doesn't add a genuine swing-and-miss weapon as he climbs, the floor is a depth arm with no real ceiling to argue over.

830402_pitcher.text: The walk rate is the whole argument here. 832562_pitcher.text: The K-BB% is the loudest thing in this profile: 24% across A+ & A, which translates to a 14.1% MLB-equivalent, right at the middle of the big-league pack. 834962_hitter.text: Seventeen home runs across AA & A+ in 370 plate appearances, with 48 walks against 79 strikeouts, is a bat-first first baseman profile that carries real weight at Double-A. A 13% walk rate and .378 OBP suggest someone who can put a lineup together rather than just feast on minor-league arms. If the contact, 21% strikeouts and .266 average, survives the jump, DePino is a low-end everyday regular at first; if it doesn't, the power alone leaves a useful bench bat.

834978_pitcher.text: The minor-league numbers are tidy — 3.4 ERA and a 1.2 WHIP across AA & A+, with 124 strikeouts in 100.3 innings, but the translation is where the profile gets honest. Everything hinges on whether the stuff plays up enough at the highest levels to keep that strikeout rate from slipping further, because if it does, the floor and the ceiling collapse into the same thing: a depth arm who fits the 40-man in a pinch but doesn't hold a rotation spot.
